title: Singly-Linked List Review
summary: Reviews singly-linked list structure, dynamic allocation, forward-only traversal, and the inability to recover a previous node's address.
main_text: Singly-Linked List Review. Singly-linked lists use structures/classes and pointers to make linked data structures. They dynamically allocate each item when the user decides to add it. Each item includes a next pointer to the following item. Traversal and iteration is only easily achieved in one direction (the forward direction). The Item struct contains an int val and an Item* next pointer. The List class has a constructor, destructor, push_back method, and a private head pointer. A key question is posed: given a temp pointer to a node, could you ever recover the address of the previous item? The answer is no, because singly-linked lists only store forward pointers. This limitation motivates the need for doubly-linked lists.
notes_text: This review establishes the critical limitation of singly-linked lists: no backward traversal. The code shown uses struct Item { int val; Item* next; }; and class List with Item* head. The memory diagram shows three nodes at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x164 with values 3, 9, and 2 respectively, each pointing forward via next pointers, with the last node's next set to NULL (0x0).

title: Doubly-Linked Lists Structure and Definition
summary: Introduces the doubly-linked list structure with prev and next pointers in each node, enabling bidirectional traversal.
main_text: Doubly-Linked Lists. A doubly-linked list includes a previous pointer in each item so that we can traverse/iterate backwards or forward. The first item's previous field should be NULL. The last item's next field should be NULL. The DLItem struct contains three fields: int val, DLItem* prev, and DLItem* next. The DLList class has a constructor, destructor, push_back method, and a private DLItem* head pointer. Each node in the list maintains two pointers: prev pointing to the preceding node and next pointing to the following node. This enables traversal in both directions from any given node, solving the limitation of singly-linked lists.
notes_text: The code defines struct DLItem { int val; DLItem* prev; DLItem* next; }; and class DLList with DLItem* head. The memory diagram shows three nodes at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x210 with values 3, 9, and 5. The first node's prev is 0x0 (NULL), and the last node's next is 0x0 (NULL). Each interior node has both prev and next pointing to its neighbors. The struct blueprint shows the DLItem layout with three fields: DLItem* prev, int val, DLItem* next.

images.description: Code snippet showing the DLItem struct with int val, DLItem* prev, and DLItem* next fields, and the DLList class declaration. A struct blueprint diagram shows the DLItem layout with prev, val, and next fields side by side.

Memory diagram showing three doubly-linked nodes at addresses 0x148, 0x1c0, and 0x210 with values 3, 9, and 5. The head pointer points to address 0x148. Each node shows DLItem* prev, int val, and DLItem* next fields. Arrows show both forward (next) and backward (prev) connections between nodes. The first node's prev is NULL and the last node's next is NULL.

title: Doubly-Linked List Add Front (Problem Setup)
summary: Poses the problem of adding a new node to the front of a doubly-linked list, emphasizing pointer update order to avoid losing information.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Add Front. Adding to the front requires you to update which pointers? Take care of the ORDER in which you update the pointers not to lose information you need. Tip: Fill in the blank fields/pointers first before changing existing ones. This slide presents the problem setup: a new node p at address 0x190 with value 12 needs to be inserted at the front of the existing list. The existing list has head pointing to address 0x148 (value 3), followed by nodes with values 9 and 5. The code area shows 'head = p; // ??' suggesting that simply setting head to p is not sufficient and more pointer updates are needed. Students must determine the correct sequence of pointer assignments.
notes_text: This is the 'before' state of the add-front operation. The key pedagogical point is that pointer update order matters critically. If you update head first, you lose the reference to the old front node. The tip to fill in blank fields first (the new node's prev and next) before modifying existing pointers (head, old front's prev) is a general strategy for linked list operations.

images.description: Diagram showing the state before insertion. A new node p at address 0x190 with value 12 has blank prev and next fields. The head pointer currently points to address 0x148. The existing list contains three nodes (3, 9, 5) with full prev/next linkage. A gray code box shows 'head = p; // ??' indicating the operation is incomplete.

title: Doubly-Linked List Add Front (Solution)
summary: Shows the complete solution for adding a node to the front, identifying the three pointers to update and their correct order in code.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Add Front. Adding to the front requires you to update which pointers? The answer is three pointers must be updated: Head, New front's next and previous, and Old front's previous. The correct code sequence is: p->prev = NULL; p->next = head; head->prev = p; (or equivalently p->next->prev = p;) head = p; The new node's prev is set to NULL since it will be the new first node. The new node's next points to the current head. The old head's prev pointer is updated to point back to the new node. Finally, head is updated to point to the new node. The order matters: head must be updated last, after using it to access the old front node.
notes_text: The completed diagram shows the new node (value 12) at address 0x190 is now the front of the list. Its prev is NULL (0x0), its next points to 0x148 (old front, value 3). The old front's prev now points to 0x190 instead of NULL. Head is updated from 0x148 to 0x190. The key insight is that we use head to set up the old front's prev pointer before reassigning head itself. The comment 'or p->next->prev = p' shows an alternative way to access the old front through p's next pointer after it has been set.

images.description: Completed memory diagram showing node p (value 12) at 0x190 inserted at the front. Dashed arrows show the new linkages: p->prev is NULL, p->next points to 0x148, the old front node's prev now points to 0x190, and head has been updated to 0x190. A code box shows the four assignment statements in order.

title: Doubly-Linked List Add Middle (Problem Setup)
summary: Poses the problem of inserting a new node into the middle of a doubly-linked list, showing the initial state before insertion.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Add Middle. Adding to the middle requires you to update which pointers? This slide presents the problem setup for middle insertion. A new node p at address 0x190 with value 12 needs to be inserted after the node pointed to by curr (which points to head at 0x148, the node with value 3). The existing list has three nodes: value 3 at 0x148, value 9 at 0x1c0, and value 5 at 0x210. Students must identify which pointers need updating and determine the correct order of operations to insert the new node between the first and second nodes.
notes_text: The curr pointer represents the node after which we want to insert. In this example, curr points to the first node (value 3). The new node will be placed between nodes with values 3 and 9. The diagram shows p pointing to a new node with blank prev and next fields, emphasizing that these must be filled in as part of the insertion.

images.description: Memory diagram showing the state before middle insertion. Head and curr both point to 0x148 (value 3). A new node p at 0x190 with value 12 has blank prev and next fields. The existing three-node list (3, 9, 5) is fully linked with prev and next pointers. An arrow from curr to p indicates where the insertion should occur.

title: Doubly-Linked List Add Middle (Solution)
summary: Shows the complete solution for middle insertion, identifying four pointers to update and providing the correct code sequence.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Add Middle. Adding to the middle requires you to update which pointers? Four pointers must be updated: Previous item's next field, Next item's previous field, New item's next field, and New item's previous field. The correct code sequence is: p->prev = curr; p->next = curr->next; curr->next->prev = p; (or equivalently p->next->prev = p;) curr->next = p; (or equivalently p->prev->next = p;) The new node's prev points to curr (the node after which we insert). The new node's next points to curr's current next. The node that was after curr has its prev updated to point to p. Finally, curr's next is updated to point to p. The order matters: curr->next must be used before it is overwritten in the last step.
notes_text: The completed diagram shows node p (value 12) at 0x190 successfully inserted between nodes at 0x148 (value 3) and 0x1c0 (value 9). The final list order is 3 -> 12 -> 9 -> 5. The alternative forms using p->next->prev and p->prev->next work because p's prev and next have already been set in the first two lines. The key ordering constraint is that curr->next->prev must be set before curr->next is reassigned, since we need curr->next to still point to the old next node.

images.description: Completed memory diagram showing node p (value 12) at 0x190 inserted between nodes at 0x148 (value 3) and 0x1c0 (value 9). All four pointer updates are shown with arrows: p->prev to 0x148, p->next to 0x1c0, node at 0x1c0 prev updated to 0x190, node at 0x148 next updated to 0x190. A code box shows the four assignment statements.

title: Doubly-Linked List Remove Middle (Problem Setup)
summary: Poses the problem of removing a node from the middle of a doubly-linked list, showing the initial state before removal.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Remove Middle. Removing from the middle requires you to update which pointers? This slide presents the problem setup for middle removal. The curr pointer at address 0x1c0 points to the middle node (value 9) which is the node to be removed. The existing list has three nodes: value 3 at 0x148, value 9 at 0x1c0, and value 5 at 0x210. A prohibition symbol (red circle with slash) is drawn over the middle node to indicate it should be removed. Students must identify which pointers need updating to bypass the removed node and properly link the remaining nodes.
notes_text: The curr pointer identifies the node to delete. Unlike singly-linked lists where you need a pointer to the node BEFORE the one to delete, doubly-linked lists allow deletion given only a pointer to the target node itself, since you can access both neighbors through curr->prev and curr->next. This is a major advantage of doubly-linked lists.

images.description: Memory diagram showing the state before middle removal. Head points to 0x148 (value 3). Curr points to 0x1c0 (value 9), the node to be removed, which has a red prohibition symbol overlaid. The three-node list (3, 9, 5) is fully linked. The prohibition symbol indicates this node will be deleted.

title: Doubly-Linked List Remove Middle (Solution)
summary: Shows the complete solution for middle removal, identifying three operations: update previous node's next, update next node's prev, and delete the node.
main_text: Doubly-Linked List Remove Middle. Removing from the middle requires you to update which pointers? Three operations are needed: Previous item's next field must be updated, Next item's previous field must be updated, and the item object must be deleted. The correct code is: curr->next->prev = curr->prev; curr->prev->next = curr->next; delete curr; The first line sets the next node's prev pointer to skip over curr and point to curr's predecessor. The second line sets the previous node's next pointer to skip over curr and point to curr's successor. After both bypass pointers are set, the node is safely deleted with delete curr. The order of the first two statements does not matter relative to each other, but both must occur before the delete.
notes_text: The completed diagram shows the middle node (value 9) at 0x1c0 removed with a prohibition symbol. The remaining two nodes (value 3 at 0x148 and value 5 at 0x210) are now directly linked: node 3's next points to 0x210, and node 5's prev points to 0x148. Head remains at 0x148. Unlike the add operations where order was critical, here the two pointer updates can happen in either order since we are only reading from curr (not modifying it) until the final delete. Memory for the removed node is freed with delete.

images.description: Completed memory diagram showing the middle node (value 9) at 0x1c0 deleted with a prohibition symbol. The remaining list has two nodes: value 3 at 0x148 with next pointing to 0x210, and value 5 at 0x210 with prev pointing to 0x148. A code box shows the three statements: curr->next->prev = curr->prev, curr->prev->next = curr->next, and delete curr.
